title: The master register
subtitle: Every square one catalogued record: white in the family’s favour, black against the other side

label.en: The family’s register — the family’s view
label.cy: Cofrestr y teulu — barn y teulu
label.es: El registro de la familia — la visión de la familia

note: The family’s view, openly so: which side each record favours is the family’s reading. Each square’s text is factual and links to its catalogue entry. Bute appears as lord of the manor, BP as registered proprietor (first registration 1982/83); where a court treated BP as owner, that is shown as the court’s view. Black squares concern acts of public bodies, companies, courts and the press.

squares.text: The name Cwm-Cedwyn appears in Llandough boundary records of 1392 — the estate's name is six centuries old.
Tithe apportionment for Llandough, Cogan and Leckwith: John Williams listed as occupier of 36 parcels, about 119 acres, plot 209 “Courtyard &c.” among them.
Cardiff Times and Cardiff & Merthyr Guardian death notices: Amy, “relict of the late Mr. John Williams, Great House farm”.
Trade directories 1868–1901 (Slater’s, Worrall’s, Owen’s, Cardiff Directory) list John Williams at “Great House farm”, Llandough.
Evening Express: the Llandough Air-rifle Club holds its Easter Monday competition “at the Great House Farm” — the house as a village meeting place.
Barry Dock News: the Llandough court leet passes a vote of sympathy with the family of “Mr. John Williams, Great House … for many years a juror of the court”.
Court leet and court baron at Llandough: a John Williams sworn on the 1910 grand jury (the court reported “no presentments” of encroachments).
Welsh Women’s Peace Petition, Llandough sheet (National Library of Wales, Petition 1/92): signed “Esther Williams — Llandough”.
Mountjoy Ltd (the Bute estate company) conveys to Western Ground Rents Ltd. Later documents call it BP’s root of title; the deed is known only from recitals and has not been examined.
The plan to Western Ground Rents’ 1939 letting to John Williams highlights the fields (Parcel B) only; the house parcel is not on it.
Western Ground Rents obtains summary judgment (Order 14) in the High Court against Frederick Buckler alone, for “the whole of the farm”; Mary Williams, living in the house, is not a party.
Writ of possession executed: the farm, except the farmhouse and garden, is taken under the 1955 judgment.
Western Mail, 7 May 1958: Mrs Mary Doreen Buckler (Mary Williams) named in the report of the public inquiry into Cardiff’s plan to take Leckwith Common for a play-field.
Cardiff seeks Leckwith Common for a play-field (public inquiry, 6 May 1958).

Mrs M. D. Buckler (Mary Williams) complains to Glamorgan County Council’s planning committee: “a Welsh case of Crichel Down” (Western Mail, 20 Nov 1958). The report carries her complaint that the water had been cut off for nearly 10 years by order of Western Ground Rents.
The family refuses Western Ground Rents’ offers of a tenancy of the house and garden, in 1959 and again in 1965 — it would not become a tenant of its own home.
Deed between Western Ground Rents, South Western Brick & Tile and Cardiff City over land now in the woodland title; the family is not a party.
Cardiff County Court orders possession of the farmhouse and garden.
School-site sale: the contract names the 25 Dec 1938 conveyance as root of title — a title passed on by recital.
Western Ground Rents sells the farm, farmhouse included, to BP Pension Trust while Mary Williams lives in the house.
Glamorgan County Council registers the green in front of the house as village green VG41, publicised by public notice only.
Outline planning permission sought for about 13 houses on the land, with an ownership certificate, while Mary Williams lives there and disputes the title.
Daily Telegraph, 16 Apr 1974: Mary Williams opens Tŷ Mawr to the public for an “open day” to save the house; quoted: “my family has lived here for more than 400 years”.
In BP Pension Trust’s possession action, Mary Williams pleads in open court that the land is hers by possession and the action against her is out of time.
Instead of trying her ownership plea, BP Pension Trust gets leave to execute the nearly twelve-year-old 1962 order.
BP Pension Trust and BP Properties send two letters letting her stay “rent free … for the rest of your life” — never asked for, never accepted in writing; the courts later read them as a licence.
Western Mail letter, “Grievous loss”: William Rees writes against the demolition of Great House Farm.
BP Pension Trust conveys the farmhouse plot to BP Properties, reserving 80-year road and sewer rights “to serve any development”, with Mary Williams still living there.
Hansard: Ted Rowlands MP criticises Western Ground Rents and the BP pension fund in the House of Commons.
The fields pass between BP companies and are first registered (WA231076), BP Properties as registered proprietor.
BP Properties applies to register the farmhouse (Form 1C, WA240304) while Mary Williams is alive and living in it.
HM Land Registry examines the farmhouse application after Mary Williams’s death on 26 Mar 1983; no record produced shows her dispute was before it.
The Commons Registration (Glamorgan) Act 1983 validates the Glamorgan common-land registers, green VG41 included.
South Wales Echo: Great House Farm noted in conservation reports by the Community Council and Vale planners.
BP Properties issues a writ for possession against her son, the occupier.
High Court in Cardiff gives judgment for BP on possession and limitation; no judgment decides title to the farmhouse.
East Vale Local Plan (Feb 1987): the buildings on the site are to be retained.
The farmhouse title is merged into the farm title (WA231076 item 14) while the appeal is still pending.
Court of Appeal dismisses the appeal. The court’s view: BP held “the paper title” and the 1974 letters made her a licensee, so it treated BP as owner.
Court of Appeal: Mary and Frederick Buckler were in adverse possession of the farmhouse from 2 Feb 1955 — the court’s own finding.
Court of Appeal calls the one-sided licence point “a new one” and notes the risk of keeping title alive “for very many years until it suits him to evict”.
Court of Appeal: Mary Williams’s 1974 ownership plea “has never been finally heard” — no court decided who owned the house.
The family petitions the House of Lords for leave to appeal: every lawful route used.
South Wales Echo tells readers she had lost three earlier High Court cases over ownership; the judgments on record decided possession, not title.
Press headline “Chainsaw farmer”: the story becomes a man at a door, not a title nobody had read.
First eviction attempt: doors smashed with poleaxes, as the farmer described it to the press.
Application 14464/88 lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights (Articles 6, 8, 13 and Protocol 1 Article 1).
Cadw inspects and photographs the farmhouse and barn for listing (photographs disclosed 11 Jun 2026).
Estates Gazette: “BP signal Welsh sales”.
The BP Pension Fund sells about 1,300 acres of Welsh land for £29,375,400; the Land Authority for Wales buys plots at Llandough.
Forced entry at Great House Farm; the outbuilding roof is removed.
South Wales Echo, “History fight to save farm”: Cadw inspection and spot-listing of the house.
The residents are evicted from their home.
Cadw writes to the responsible Minister about spot-listing Great House Farm.
South Wales Echo: the evicted farmer is taken from a hospital bed to face an assault charge (later dropped).
South Wales Echo: villagers’ anger at the demolition of the Llandough farmhouse.
A Cardiff court refuses the injunction to stop BP Properties destroying the house while Cadw is still deciding on listing.
Western Mail names BP Properties as “the owners of the land”, as plain fact.
The 800-year-old farmhouse is demolished: “Tears flow as 800 year-old farm house is razed at last”.
South Wales Echo: a councillor calls the demolition decision “disgusting”.
Sites and Monuments Record card PRN 02038s: “building destroyed by owners”.
Barry magistrates: the charge brought against the evicted farmer is dropped.
South Wales Echo: Vale councillors authorise legal action against BP Properties over the demolition.
European Commission of Human Rights declares 14464/88 inadmissible, finding no “possession” because the British courts held the property “belonged to another”.
Outline permission for housing on the site (89/01396/OUT), then 20 detached houses (1992).
The Glamorgan Village Book (presented to Dinas Powys Library, 19 Nov 1993) gives Great House Farm a place in the county’s village history.
Ministry of Justice FOI “BP vs Buckler 1987”: the court records are “not held”.
The family takes its case that the register is mistaken through HM Land Registry’s complaint stages — the lawful route, in the open.
The Strasbourg case file is reported destroyed under the Court’s retention policy.
Cadw refuses a request for the July–December 1988 listing papers as a repeat request (FOIA s.14(2)).
Vale of Glamorgan Council: no substantive response to the FOI request on application 2020/01590/HYB.

topic.en: House opened to the public — the Glamorgan Village Book
topic.cy: Agor y tŷ i’r cyhoedd — The Glamorgan Village Book
topic.es: Casa abierta al público — The Glamorgan Village Book

to_be_sourced.status: Book found in the catalogue (presented to Dinas Powys Library, 19 Nov 1993): cover, library page and two printed pages are held as photographs, but no transcription on file carries a statement that the house was opened to the public. The 1974 open day itself is on the board (Daily Telegraph, 16 Apr 1974).
to_be_sourced.needs: A clear photograph of the page that mentions the opening, with the book’s title page.

to_be_sourced.status: No record yet. Requests are out: Glamorgan Archives (no reply), Amgueddfa Cymru – Museum Wales (“not held”), National Library of Wales (partial disclosure, nothing on provenance).
to_be_sourced.needs: An inventory, sale catalogue, receipt, valuation or dated photograph naming Cardiff Castle as the source of the pieces.

to_be_sourced.status: No record on file names the family as gentry. Nearest on the board: “Mr. John Williams, Great House … for many years a juror of the court” (1908).
to_be_sourced.needs: A will, probate entry, directory “gentry / private residents” list, parish office (churchwarden, overseer) or other record describing the family’s rank.

topic.en: Esther Williams’s petition and her link to Mary
topic.cy: Deiseb Esther Williams a’i chysylltiad â Mary
topic.es: La petición de Esther Williams y su vínculo con Mary

to_be_sourced.status: On the board: “Esther Williams — Llandough” on the 1923 Welsh Women’s Peace Petition. The catalogue does not yet show that this Esther is Mary’s mother, or any other petition of hers.
to_be_sourced.needs: A birth, marriage or census entry linking Esther and Mary; a copy of any other petition Esther made.

topic.en: Mary Williams’s 1958 “Welsh Crichel Down” — full text
topic.cy: “Crichel Down Cymreig” Mary Williams, 1958 — y testun llawn
topic.es: El “Crichel Down galés” de Mary Williams, 1958 — texto completo

to_be_sourced.status: On the board from the Western Mail snippet. The full article, the county planning committee minutes and the verbatim inquiry report (days 20–24) are not yet read.
to_be_sourced.needs: The full Western Mail page of 20 Nov 1958 and the committee minutes of 19 Nov 1958.

topic.en: John Williams in the manor court books
topic.cy: John Williams yn llyfrau llys y faenor
topic.es: John Williams en los libros del tribunal señorial

to_be_sourced.status: Press reports place a John Williams of Great House on the court leet jury. The court books themselves (to 1937) are catalogued but unread. A Llandough constable “Jenkin M. Williams” (1913, 1917) is not linked to Great House, so he is not on the board.
to_be_sourced.needs: Glamorgan Archives DB/M/1–9 (court books) and the presentments to 1934 — free to view in the reading room.

topic.es: Manos limpias (ante el tribunal de equidad)

to_be_sourced.status: No single record states it. The “honour” squares show the family taking each step openly and by the lawful route (public inquiry, open day, plea in court, appeals, Strasbourg, the Registry’s complaint stages).
to_be_sourced.needs: Nothing to find: it is argued from the honour squares.

to_be_sourced.status: No deed in hand on either side. The 1938 conveyance and its plan are the deciding document; the Land Registry’s reply to the subject access request is due 28 Oct 2026.
to_be_sourced.needs: The 25 Dec 1938 conveyance with plan, or the family’s own title papers.
